cards.title: What is the virtual DOM?
cards.content: React keeps an in-memory snapshot of the UI called the virtual DOM. On every render, a new virtual DOM tree is produced and compared against the previous one. Only the differences are applied to the real DOM, minimizing expensive browser operations.

cards.question: What is the time complexity of React's diffing algorithm?
options: O(n³) — comparing every node against every other node
O(n²) — quadratic tree comparison
O(n) — linear, using heuristics
O(log n) — binary search on the tree
cards.answer: O(n) — linear, using heuristics
cards.explanation: React achieves O(n) by applying two heuristics: different types always produce a full subtree swap, and the key prop identifies list items by identity.

cards.title: The two core diffing heuristics
cards.content: 1. Different element type → React tears down the entire old subtree and mounts a fresh one, destroying all descendant state. 2. Same element type → React updates only the changed props and reuses the existing DOM node.

cards.question: When a parent component changes its child's element type from <div> to <section>, React will try to reuse the existing DOM node.
cards.explanation: React always does a full subtree remount when element types differ. The old subtree is unmounted (destroying state), and a brand new one is mounted.

cards.title: Spot the bug
cards.prompt: The following list renders incorrectly after reordering items. Why?
cards.answer: Using array index as key ties identity to position. When items reorder, React sees the same keys in new positions and updates props instead of moving nodes — causing state mismatches and unnecessary re-renders. Fix: use a stable unique ID as the key.

cards.question: What is the React Fiber architecture primarily designed to solve?
options: Make the virtual DOM faster to create
Allow reconciliation work to be paused and resumed, enabling priority-based scheduling
Replace the virtual DOM with direct DOM manipulation
Reduce the bundle size of React
cards.answer: Allow reconciliation work to be paused and resumed, enabling priority-based scheduling
cards.explanation: Fiber breaks render work into small units that can be interrupted. High-priority updates (e.g. user input) can pause low-priority work (e.g. background data). The commit phase, however, is always synchronous.

cards.title: Render phase vs. commit phase
cards.content: The render phase is interruptible — React builds the new fiber tree and calculates changes. The commit phase is synchronous and uninterruptible — React applies all DOM mutations at once, then fires useLayoutEffect (synchronously) and useEffect (after paint).

cards.question: Why does wrapping a component in a different component type on every render cause performance issues?
cards.answer: React sees a new element type each render, triggering a full subtree unmount and remount. All child state is lost and components go through full mount lifecycles. Example: defining a component inside another component's render function.

cards.title: React.memo — the outer gate
cards.content: React.memo is a higher-order component. It wraps a component and skips re-rendering it if all props are shallowly equal to the previous render. It only prevents re-renders caused by the parent — if internal state or context changes, the component still re-renders.

cards.question: What does useCallback memoize?
options: The return value of a function
The function reference itself
The component render output
The props object passed to a component
cards.answer: The function reference itself
cards.explanation: useCallback returns the same function object across renders as long as dependencies haven't changed. This is useful when passing callbacks to React.memo-wrapped children, since a new function reference on every render would break memoization.

cards.question: useMemo and useCallback are always worth adding to improve performance.
cards.explanation: Memoization has a cost — it stores values and runs dependency comparisons on every render. Premature memoization adds complexity with no benefit. Only reach for these hooks when you've identified a real performance bottleneck.

cards.title: Fix the broken memoization
cards.prompt: Child is wrapped in React.memo but still re-renders on every parent render. What is wrong?
cards.answer: handleClick is recreated as a new function reference on every Parent render. React.memo compares props by shallow equality — a new function reference means the prop 'changed', so Child re-renders. Fix: wrap handleClick with useCallback(() => { console.log('clicked'); }, []).

cards.question: When should you use useMemo?
options: For every derived value in a component
When passing a callback to a child component
For expensive computations whose result shouldn't be recalculated on every render
To prevent a component from re-rendering
cards.answer: For expensive computations whose result shouldn't be recalculated on every render
cards.explanation: useMemo caches a computed value and only recalculates it when dependencies change. Classic use cases: filtering/sorting large arrays, complex mathematical operations, or building objects that would otherwise cause downstream re-renders.

cards.question: What is the difference between useMemo and useCallback in terms of what they return?
cards.answer: useMemo returns the result of calling the function — the computed value. useCallback returns the function itself without calling it. useCallback(fn, deps) is equivalent to useMemo(() => fn, deps).

cards.title: Choose the right hook
cards.prompt: For each scenario, decide whether to use useMemo, useCallback, React.memo, or nothing:
scenarios: Filtering a 10,000-item list based on a search string
A pure presentational Button component that receives an onClick prop
An event handler passed down two levels to a memoized child
A simple counter that displays count + 1
cards.answer: 1. useMemo — expensive derived value. 2. React.memo — skip re-renders when props haven't changed. 3. useCallback — stabilize the function reference so React.memo on the child isn't defeated. 4. Nothing — the computation is trivial; memoization overhead exceeds any benefit.

cards.question: React.memo prevents a component from re-rendering when its own internal state changes.
cards.explanation: React.memo only compares incoming props. If the component calls useState or useReducer internally and state changes, it re-renders regardless of React.memo. Memo only guards against parent-triggered re-renders.

cards.title: How the Context API works
cards.content: createContext creates a context object with a Provider component. The Provider accepts a value prop that is broadcast to any descendant calling useContext with that context. When the value reference changes, React walks the tree and re-renders every consumer — bypassing React.memo entirely. This makes context ideal for low-frequency globals like theme or auth state.

cards.question: What triggers a re-render in every useContext consumer?
options: Any state change anywhere in the app
The Provider's value prop changing by reference
A parent component re-rendering above the Provider
The consumer component's own state changing
cards.answer: The Provider's value prop changing by reference
cards.explanation: React compares the new and previous context value with Object.is. If the reference changes — even if the data is structurally identical — all consumers re-render. This is why inline objects like value={{ user, setUser }} in JSX are dangerous.

cards.question: Wrapping a context consumer with React.memo will prevent it from re-rendering when the context value changes.
cards.explanation: React.memo only guards against prop changes from a parent. Context updates bypass memo entirely — a memoized component will still re-render whenever the context value it consumes changes.

cards.title: Spot the performance pitfall
cards.prompt: Every component consuming AuthContext re-renders on every keystroke in the search bar. Why?
cards.answer: App re-renders on every search keystroke, creating a new { user, setUser } object reference each time. Even though user hasn't changed, the new object reference causes all AuthContext consumers to re-render. Fix: memoize the value — const authValue = useMemo(() => ({ user, setUser }), [user]) — or lift the search state out of App into a separate component so App doesn't re-render on keystrokes.

cards.title: Splitting contexts by update frequency
cards.content: A single large context that holds both slow-changing data (e.g. theme) and fast-changing data (e.g. scroll position) will re-render all consumers whenever either changes. The fix is to split them into separate contexts — consumers only subscribe to the context they need, so a scroll update doesn't repaint theme-dependent components.

cards.question: You have a UserContext that stores the full user object. A deeply nested Avatar component only needs user.avatarUrl. What problem might arise and how would you address it?
cards.answer: If any other field on user changes (e.g. user.lastSeen), Avatar re-renders even though avatarUrl didn't change. Solutions: (1) split the context so Avatar consumes a dedicated AvatarContext, (2) use a selector pattern with a state manager like Zustand or Redux, or (3) derive the value in the consuming component and memoize it — though context itself still triggers the re-render first.

cards.question: Which of the following is the safest pattern for a context that provides both state and a setter?
options: value={{ theme, setTheme }} directly in JSX
Separate ThemeContext for the value and ThemeDispatchContext for the setter
Storing theme in a ref instead of state
Using a single context updated with Object.assign
cards.answer: Separate ThemeContext for the value and ThemeDispatchContext for the setter
cards.explanation: Setters (dispatch functions) never change between renders. Splitting them into their own context means components that only dispatch actions never re-render when the state value changes — a common pattern recommended in the React docs.

cards.title: Refactor for performance
cards.prompt: Refactor this context so that components consuming only the dispatch function do not re-render when count changes.

cards.question: Context is a good replacement for a state management library like Zustand or Redux in all cases.
cards.explanation: Context lacks built-in selectors — you can't subscribe to a slice of context state. Every consumer re-renders on any value change. For high-frequency or granular state, dedicated libraries with selector support (Zustand, Redux Toolkit, Jotai) are significantly more performant.

cards.title: Why React maintains a virtual UI tree
cards.content: Touching the real DOM is one of the most expensive things a web app can do, so React avoids it whenever possible. Instead, it represents the UI as a lightweight JavaScript object tree — the virtual DOM. Each render produces a fresh tree, which React then reconciles against the previous one to figure out the minimal set of mutations needed before any actual DOM call is made.

cards.title: The virtual DOM, in plain terms
cards.content: Think of the virtual DOM as a draft of the page that lives in memory. When state changes, React draws a new draft and lays it next to the old one, circles only the differences, and ships those edits to the browser. The browser never sees the drafts — only the final, surgically-applied changes — which is what makes updates cheap.

cards.title: Virtual DOM: not magic, just bookkeeping
cards.content: The virtual DOM isn't a faster DOM — it's a diffing buffer. React keeps two plain-object snapshots of your component tree: the one currently on screen and the one your render functions just produced. A reconciliation pass walks both trees in parallel, and only the nodes that genuinely differ are translated into imperative DOM operations like appendChild or setAttribute.

cards.title: The two rules that drive React's diff
cards.content: Rule one: if the element type at a given position changes (say <ul> becomes <ol>, or <ComponentA> becomes <ComponentB>), React doesn't try to be clever — it throws away the entire old subtree, including all hooks and state inside it, and builds the new one from scratch. Rule two: if the type matches, React keeps the existing instance alive and only patches whatever props or attributes actually changed.

cards.title: How React decides: reuse or rebuild?
cards.content: At each position in the tree React asks a single question: 'is the element type the same as last time?' A 'yes' means update-in-place — same DOM node, same component instance, just patched props. A 'no' triggers a hard reset: unmount the old subtree (state, refs, effects and all), then mount the new one fresh. This is why swapping a wrapper element can quietly nuke everything below it.

cards.title: Type identity is everything
cards.content: React's diffing leans on one shortcut to stay linear: it never tries to match nodes across different types. A <div> and a <span> at the same position are treated as completely unrelated trees, even if their children are identical. Same goes for components — <Foo /> and <Bar /> are strangers to React, which is why moving a child between two different parent component types resets all of its state.

cards.title: The two phases of a React update
cards.content: Every update splits into two phases. First the render phase, where React calls your components, builds a new fiber tree, and works out what changed — this phase can be paused, restarted, or thrown away entirely, so it must be pure. Then the commit phase, a single synchronous burst where React writes the DOM mutations, runs useLayoutEffect, and finally schedules useEffect to fire after the browser paints.

cards.title: Why render is interruptible but commit isn't
cards.content: The render phase is just JavaScript producing a description of the next UI — no user-visible side effects yet — so React feels free to slice it up, yield to the browser, and even discard half-finished work if something more urgent comes in. The commit phase is the opposite: once React starts mutating the DOM, stopping halfway would leave the page in a torn state, so it runs to completion in one synchronous shot.

cards.title: Effects timing, render vs commit
cards.content: Knowing the phase boundary clears up effect timing. Anything inside a component body runs during render and must be pure. useLayoutEffect fires synchronously inside the commit phase, after the DOM is updated but before the browser paints — perfect for measuring layout. useEffect is deferred until after paint, which is why it's the safe default for data fetching and subscriptions.

cards.title: React.memo, the prop-change firewall
cards.content: React.memo wraps a component and intercepts its renders triggered by a parent. Before re-rendering, it shallow-compares the new props against the previous ones; if nothing changed, it bails out and reuses last render's output. It does not freeze the component — internal state updates, hook changes, and consumed context will all still cause a re-render, because React.memo only guards the parent-to-child boundary.

cards.title: What React.memo actually skips
cards.content: A common misread of React.memo is that it 'makes a component pure' or 'caches its output'. It does neither. What it really does is add a gate at the top of the component: when the parent re-renders, React checks each prop for shallow equality, and if they all match, the component's body is skipped this round. State changes, context changes, and force-updates ignore that gate entirely.

cards.title: React.memo: a higher-order component, not a hook
cards.content: Unlike useMemo and useCallback, React.memo isn't called inside a component — it wraps one. You hand it a component definition and get back a new component that performs a shallow props comparison before each render. It's purely an optimization, and only helps when the parent re-renders frequently while the child's props stay equal by reference — pass it a fresh object or inline arrow function and the memoization is silently defeated.

cards.title: Context, end to end
cards.content: createContext gives you back two things bundled together: a Provider component and a hook target. Anywhere a Provider sits in the tree, every descendant that calls useContext(MyContext) reads the current value prop. When that value changes by reference, React walks down from the Provider and re-renders each consumer — and importantly, it does so even through React.memo boundaries. That's why context fits theme, locale, or current user well, but struggles with rapidly-changing data.

cards.title: How useContext finds its value
cards.content: Each context object carries an internal slot that holds the value of the nearest Provider above the consumer. When you call useContext(MyContext), React climbs the fiber tree at render time, finds that Provider, and hands you its current value prop. There's no subscription you need to set up; React tracks the dependency for you and schedules a re-render on every consumer whenever the Provider's value changes by reference.

cards.title: Context: broadcast, not selector
cards.content: Context is best thought of as a broadcast channel. The Provider publishes a single value and every subscriber receives the same payload, in full, whenever it changes. There's no built-in way to subscribe to just a slice of that value — if the Provider's reference changes, every useContext caller re-renders, period. This 'all or nothing' model is what makes it powerful for global concerns and painful for high-frequency state.

cards.title: Split contexts by how often they change
cards.content: Mixing rarely-changing values (theme, current user) with frequently-changing ones (mouse position, scroll offset) in the same context means every fast update re-renders every slow consumer too. The standard remedy is to split the data into multiple contexts grouped by update cadence, so each consumer only subscribes to the stream of changes it actually cares about.

cards.title: One context, one cadence
cards.content: A good rule of thumb when designing context: every consumer of a context will re-render at the rate of that context's fastest-changing field. So if you put a once-per-session value next to a once-per-frame value in the same Provider, you've effectively promoted the slow consumers to render every frame. Splitting them into independent contexts restores the original update frequency for each set of consumers.

cards.title: Why one giant AppContext usually backfires
cards.content: It's tempting to expose everything — auth, theme, feature flags, live data — through a single AppContext. The problem shows up later: a tiny update to one field rewrites the Provider's value reference, and every component anywhere in the tree that called useContext(AppContext) re-renders, regardless of which field it actually reads. Breaking the monolith into smaller, purpose-specific contexts keeps re-renders scoped to the consumers that genuinely care.
cards._note: Variant of card 21 — same idea, framed around the antipattern.

cards.question: Why is React's diffing algorithm able to run in O(n) time across the component tree?
options: Because React caches the previous render's DOM nodes in a hash map keyed by element type
Because it relies on heuristics — different types swap whole subtrees, and keys identify list children — instead of a fully general tree-diff
Because reconciliation only runs on the changed subtree, never the whole tree
Because the virtual DOM is stored as a flat array, not a tree
cards.answer: Because it relies on heuristics — different types swap whole subtrees, and keys identify list children — instead of a fully general tree-diff
cards.explanation: A truly general tree-to-tree diff is O(n³). React sidesteps that by assuming the developer follows two rules: elements of different types yield different trees, and stable keys identify children across renders. With those assumptions, a single pass over the tree is enough — hence linear time.

cards.question: The naive optimal tree-diff is O(n³). What allows React to do it in O(n) without sacrificing correctness in practice?
options: It uses memoization to cache subtree comparisons across renders
It runs diffing on a Web Worker so the main thread isn't blocked
It substitutes a heuristic-driven walk (type-equality shortcut + key-based child matching) for a fully general diff, accepting suboptimal results when the rules are violated
It compresses the virtual DOM into a binary trie before comparison
cards.answer: It substitutes a heuristic-driven walk (type-equality shortcut + key-based child matching) for a fully general diff, accepting suboptimal results when the rules are violated
cards.explanation: React doesn't compute the theoretically minimal edit script — it computes a good-enough one in linear time by trusting two heuristics. When those heuristics are wrong (e.g. unstable keys or unnecessarily-swapped wrapper types), you get extra mounts/unmounts: correct output, but worse performance.

cards.question: Which statement most precisely describes the complexity of React's reconciliation?
options: O(n) amortized, O(n³) worst-case when keys collide
O(n log n), because React internally sorts children by key before diffing
O(n) where n is the number of elements, achieved by refusing to diff across element-type boundaries and by using keys as identity hints for siblings
O(n²) in the general case, reduced to O(n) only when React.memo is applied to every child
cards.answer: O(n) where n is the number of elements, achieved by refusing to diff across element-type boundaries and by using keys as identity hints for siblings
cards.explanation: The complexity is genuinely O(n) — not amortized, not conditional on memo. The two heuristics (type equality cuts the search at each position; keys match siblings by identity) are what reduce the problem from cubic to linear. React.memo is unrelated; it's a separate render-skipping optimization.

cards.question: What problem was the Fiber rewrite introduced to address?
options: Long synchronous reconciliation passes blocking the main thread, with no way to prioritize urgent updates over background ones
Excessive memory usage from storing two full virtual DOM trees in memory
The need to support multiple renderers (DOM, Native) from a single React core
Slow initial bundle parse times caused by the old stack reconciler
cards.answer: Long synchronous reconciliation passes blocking the main thread, with no way to prioritize urgent updates over background ones
cards.explanation: The pre-Fiber 'stack' reconciler did all its work in one uninterruptible recursive call. A large tree could block input handling for hundreds of milliseconds. Fiber breaks rendering into small units that can yield to the browser and be reordered by priority, enabling features like concurrent rendering and Suspense.

cards.question: Which of the following best captures what Fiber changed about how React works?
options: Fiber replaced the virtual DOM with direct DOM mutation, removing the diffing step entirely
Fiber made both the render and commit phases asynchronous and interruptible
Fiber re-implemented reconciliation as a cooperative, unit-of-work scheduler — the render phase became interruptible and prioritizable, while the commit phase remained synchronous
Fiber turned every component into a coroutine so its render function can suspend and resume mid-execution
cards.answer: Fiber re-implemented reconciliation as a cooperative, unit-of-work scheduler — the render phase became interruptible and prioritizable, while the commit phase remained synchronous
cards.explanation: Fiber kept the virtual DOM and the two-phase model; what changed is how the render phase executes. It now processes one fiber (one unit of work) at a time and can yield to the browser between units. Commit is still atomic — partial DOM mutations would be a disaster.

cards.question: A senior dev claims: 'Fiber is what made React fast.' What's the most accurate critique of that statement?
options: It's correct — Fiber introduced incremental DOM updates, which the previous reconciler didn't have

It's misleading — Fiber doesn't make raw rendering faster; it makes it interruptible and prioritizable, so urgent updates aren't blocked behind less important ones. Throughput is roughly the same; responsiveness is what improved
It's wrong — Fiber actually made initial renders slower due to scheduling overhead, and is only beneficial for concurrent features
It's correct — Fiber replaced the O(n³) diff with an O(n) diff, which is the main source of the speedup
cards.answer: It's misleading — Fiber doesn't make raw rendering faster; it makes it interruptible and prioritizable, so urgent updates aren't blocked behind less important ones. Throughput is roughly the same; responsiveness is what improved
cards.explanation: The O(n) diff predates Fiber. Fiber's contribution is scheduling: total CPU work is unchanged (or slightly higher due to bookkeeping), but it can now be spread out and reprioritized. 'Fast' in a perceived-latency sense, not a throughput sense.

cards.question: What does useCallback actually return?
options: The cached result of calling the function
The same function reference across renders, as long as its dependencies are unchanged
A new function that internally memoizes its return value
A ref containing the function, so its identity can be mutated without re-rendering
cards.answer: The same function reference across renders, as long as its dependencies are unchanged
cards.explanation: useCallback memoizes the function itself, not its output. As long as the dependency array stays shallow-equal, you get back the exact same function instance you got last render — useful for keeping reference equality stable when passing callbacks to memoized children.

cards.question: Which of the following is the most accurate description of useCallback(fn, deps)?
options: It's syntactic sugar for useMemo(() => fn(), deps)
It returns the memoized invocation result of fn
It's equivalent to useMemo(() => fn, deps) — it caches the function reference, not the call
It prevents fn from being redefined on subsequent renders by hoisting it out of the component
cards.answer: It's equivalent to useMemo(() => fn, deps) — it caches the function reference, not the call
cards.explanation: useCallback and useMemo are siblings. useCallback(fn, deps) is literally the same as useMemo(() => fn, deps): both keep something stable across renders until deps change. The difference is that useMemo's factory is expected to compute a value, while useCallback's payload is the function itself.

cards.question: A teammate writes: `const handler = useCallback(() => doThing(value), []);`. What is the subtle bug?
options: useCallback can't be used with arrow functions; it requires a named function declaration
The empty dependency array causes the closure to capture the initial `value` forever — when `value` updates, `handler` still references the stale one. The fix is to add `value` to the deps
useCallback always recomputes regardless of deps, so this is just dead overhead
useCallback returns undefined on first render, so `handler` will throw when invoked
cards.answer: The empty dependency array causes the closure to capture the initial `value` forever — when `value` updates, `handler` still references the stale one. The fix is to add `value` to the deps
cards.explanation: useCallback stabilizes the function reference, but the function still closes over whatever was in scope when it was created. With deps = [], that snapshot is taken once on mount and never refreshed — a classic stale-closure bug. Listing `value` in the deps array makes useCallback rebuild the function whenever `value` changes.

cards.question: Which scenario is the textbook case for reaching for useMemo?
options: Stopping a child component from re-rendering when its parent updates
Caching the result of an expensive synchronous computation (e.g. filtering a 10k-row table) so it isn't redone on every render
Persisting a value across remounts of the same component
Avoiding an effect re-running when only unrelated state changes
cards.answer: Caching the result of an expensive synchronous computation (e.g. filtering a 10k-row table) so it isn't redone on every render
cards.explanation: useMemo's purpose is to skip recomputing a derived value when its inputs haven't changed. Heavy filters, sorts, and reductions are the canonical fit. Preventing child re-renders is React.memo's job, persisting across unmounts requires external storage, and effect dependencies are governed by useEffect's own dep array.

cards.question: When is useMemo genuinely worth reaching for?
options: On every derived value, to follow best practice

When the computation is measurably expensive on each render, OR when the resulting value's reference identity matters for downstream memoization (e.g. it's passed to React.memo or used as an effect dep)
Only when the value is an object, because primitives don't need memoization
Whenever the component re-renders more than a few times per second
cards.answer: When the computation is measurably expensive on each render, OR when the resulting value's reference identity matters for downstream memoization (e.g. it's passed to React.memo or used as an effect dep)
cards.explanation: There are really two reasons to use useMemo. The obvious one is CPU savings on heavy work. The subtler one is reference stability — if you pass `{ a, b }` to a memoized child or to an effect's dep array, a fresh object each render defeats the optimization. Memoizing the object preserves referential identity until inputs change.

cards.question: Which of these usages of useMemo is most likely to be a net negative?
options: Memoizing the result of `array.filter(x => x.active)` on a 50,000-item array used by a chart
Memoizing `{ x, y }` that's passed as a prop to a React.memo-wrapped <Marker />
Memoizing a primitive like `useMemo(() => count + 1, [count])` returned directly in JSX
Memoizing an object passed into a useEffect dependency array
cards.answer: Memoizing a primitive like `useMemo(() => count + 1, [count])` returned directly in JSX
cards.explanation: The first option is a real CPU win; the second and fourth protect downstream reference equality. Memoizing `count + 1` does neither — primitives compare by value, the computation is one addition, and useMemo itself has bookkeeping overhead (storing the value, comparing deps). Pure noise, slightly negative on balance.

cards.question: Which event causes every component using useContext(MyContext) to re-render?
options: Any state update anywhere above the consumer in the tree
The MyContext.Provider's `value` prop changing by reference (compared with Object.is)
The consumer's own state updating
A sibling of the Provider re-rendering
cards.answer: The MyContext.Provider's `value` prop changing by reference (compared with Object.is)
cards.explanation: Context re-renders are driven solely by reference change of the Provider's `value` prop, compared via Object.is. Identical contents in a freshly-allocated object will still trigger every consumer — which is exactly why inlining `value={{ ...something }}` in JSX is a well-known foot-gun.

cards.question: Two renders of a Provider produce values that are deep-equal but not the same reference. What happens to consumers?
options: Nothing — React performs a shallow equality check on the value's fields and bails out
Nothing — React deep-compares context values to avoid spurious re-renders
Every consumer re-renders, because React compares context values with Object.is, which is reference equality for objects
Consumers re-render only if they're not wrapped in React.memo
cards.answer: Every consumer re-renders, because React compares context values with Object.is, which is reference equality for objects
cards.explanation: React intentionally avoids deep or shallow comparison of context values — both would be expensive and ambiguous. It uses Object.is, which for objects is plain reference equality. A new object that 'looks the same' is, as far as context is concerned, a completely new value, and all consumers re-render.

cards.question: A component reads `const { user } = useContext(AuthContext)`. The Provider's value is `useMemo(() => ({ user, token }), [user, token])`. Only `token` changes. What happens to the component?
options: It does not re-render, because it destructured `user` and React tracks per-field subscriptions
It does not re-render, because useMemo prevented the value reference from changing
It re-renders, because the Provider's value reference changed (the useMemo recomputed when `token` changed), and context has no concept of per-field subscription
It re-renders only if it's not wrapped in React.memo
cards.answer: It re-renders, because the Provider's value reference changed (the useMemo recomputed when `token` changed), and context has no concept of per-field subscription
cards.explanation: This is the core limitation of context. There are no selectors — consumers can't subscribe to individual fields. When `token` updates, useMemo produces a new object (its dep changed), the Provider's value reference changes, and React notifies every consumer regardless of which fields they actually read. The fix is splitting AuthContext into UserContext and TokenContext, or using a library with selector support.

cards.question: You're designing a context that exposes both a state value and a setter. Which pattern minimizes unnecessary re-renders?
options: Provide them together: `<Ctx.Provider value={{ state, setState }}>` to keep the API simple
Use one context but memoize the value with `useMemo(() => ({ state, setState }), [state])`
Split into two contexts: a ValueContext holding `state`, and a DispatchContext holding `setState`. Components that only need to dispatch won't re-render when `state` changes
Store `state` in a ref and expose only the ref through context, so no re-renders ever happen
cards.answer: Split into two contexts: a ValueContext holding `state`, and a DispatchContext holding `setState`. Components that only need to dispatch won't re-render when `state` changes
cards.explanation: Setters returned by useState/useReducer are reference-stable across renders. By giving them their own context, dispatch-only consumers subscribe to a value that effectively never changes, so they're never re-rendered by state updates. This is a pattern explicitly recommended in the React docs (and used internally by libraries like Redux's react-redux).

cards.question: A teammate proposes: 'Just put state in a ref and expose the ref through context — that way nothing ever re-renders.' What's the strongest objection?
options: Refs can't be put inside context values; React will throw at runtime

Mutating a ref's `.current` doesn't notify React, so consumers won't re-render when the value changes — which means the UI will silently desync from state. Refs are for values React shouldn't track, not for shared state
It works, but only if every consumer is wrapped in React.memo, otherwise they re-render anyway
Refs are reset on every render, so the value would be lost
cards.answer: Mutating a ref's `.current` doesn't notify React, so consumers won't re-render when the value changes — which means the UI will silently desync from state. Refs are for values React shouldn't track, not for shared state
cards.explanation: The proposal does eliminate re-renders — by eliminating reactivity entirely. Refs are an escape hatch for data React explicitly should not track (DOM nodes, timer IDs, mutable instance variables). Using them for shared application state means updates won't propagate to the UI. The right tool for 'shared state without context churn' is either context splitting or an external store (Zustand, Jotai, Redux) with proper selectors.

cards.question: Which of the following is the *single* safest claim about a Provider that exposes both state and a stable dispatch?
options: Memoizing the value object with `useMemo(() => ({ state, dispatch }), [state, dispatch])` is functionally equivalent to splitting into two contexts
Wrapping every consumer in React.memo lets you safely keep state and dispatch in the same context with no perf cost

Splitting into a StateContext and a DispatchContext is the only pattern that prevents dispatch-only consumers from re-rendering when state changes — because dispatch's reference stability isn't enough on its own when it's bundled with state in a single object
Both useReducer's dispatch and useState's setter are reference-stable, so consumers of either will never re-render regardless of how the context is structured
cards.answer: Splitting into a StateContext and a DispatchContext is the only pattern that prevents dispatch-only consumers from re-rendering when state changes — because dispatch's reference stability isn't enough on its own when it's bundled with state in a single object
cards.explanation: Subtle but important. Yes, `dispatch` is reference-stable. But if you bundle it as `{ state, dispatch }`, the *object* gets a new reference whenever `state` changes — and context compares the object, not its fields. Memoizing doesn't help either, since the memo's deps include `state`. The only way to truly insulate dispatch-only consumers is to put `dispatch` behind its own context, where the value literally never changes.
